title: Massive Stars School Opens in Tenerife as Models Disagree on Binary Origin of Black Hole Mergers
excerpt: Massive stars are the focus as the Canary Islands Winter School of Astrophysics opens in Tenerife, where about 100 early-career researchers will study why binary star simulations disagree on black hole mergers: one code puts the traditional channel under 20% of high-metallicity mergers, others say
content:
The Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias (IAC) opened its 37th Winter School of Astrophysics on Monday in La Laguna, Tenerife, putting just over 100 students and early-career researchers through two weeks of training on an unsettled question: how pairs of massive stars become the merging black holes that LIGO, Virgo and KAGRA detect. The school runs through Friday, Nov. 27, at the IACTEC building, and it matters to anyone who follows gravitational-wave results because claims about where merging black holes come from depend on stellar-evolution codes that do not yet agree with one another.

The school opens between catalogs. The LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration's fifth catalog, released May 26, lists 390 confirmed detections since 2015, including 161 new signals from the second part of its fourth observing run. The collaboration said the final portion of that run is set for public release in December. The detectors are now in a period of upgrades and commissioning, and a Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics page currently targets mid-January 2027 for a six-month observing run called IR1. The collaboration's own April 2026 plan update had pointed to late October or mid-November 2026.

Sergio Simón-Díaz, an IAC researcher, coordinates the school with Gastón Escobar of the IAC and Sara R. Berlanas and Michael Abdul-Masih of the Universidad de La Laguna (ULL), according to the IAC's preview of the school. IAC Director Valentín Martínez Pillet and Jonay I. González Hernández, coordinator of the IAC's Research Area, welcomed participants and formally opened the school. The program has ten lectures and a set of hands-on tutorials, listed on the IAC event page. The observational lectures cover optical, ultraviolet and infrared views of massive stars (Miriam García), stellar-mass black holes (Jorge Casares), X-rays (Montserrat Armas Padilla), gravitational-wave events (Nadia Blagorodnova) and core-collapse supernovae and related transients (Takashi Moriya). Participants come from about 20 countries, about half are women, and about 10 attend remotely.

Why Do Binary Star Models Disagree on Black Hole Mergers?

Most massive stars do not live alone. A 2012 Science study led by H. Sana found that more than 70% of massive stars will exchange mass with a companion, which leads to a merger in about one-third of cases. A 2025 Nature Astronomy survey led by Hugues Sana of KU Leuven, with IAC and La Laguna participation, tracked 139 O-type stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a galaxy whose metal content is about one-fifth of the Sun's. The team found that 45% of them show velocity changes that mark a close companion, and after correcting for observational biases, at least 70% are close binaries.

Abdul-Masih said the school gives binary interactions particular weight because most massive stars are born in multiple-star systems. He lectures on characterizing massive binaries, including systems that pair an OB star with a black hole or neutron star, and teaches the tutorial on quantitative spectroscopy of massive binaries. The disagreement starts after that. Population-synthesis codes simulate huge numbers of stellar pairs to predict how many end as merging compact objects, and they do not agree on the answer. Giuliano Iorio of the University of Barcelona's Institut de Ciències del Cosmos (ICCUB), who gives the school's lecture on population synthesis and its link to gravitational-wave events, led a 2023 study that used the SEVN code to evolve about 1.2 billion binaries. At high metallicity, under 20% of merging black holes and neutron-star binaries formed through the main traditional channel in that study, while other authors reported more than 70%.

Matching the settings does not close that gap. The SEVN team reported that its formation channels and merger efficiencies differ from other codes even when the same binary-evolution parameters are used. Changing the convective overshooting parameter and the pair-instability model also moves the maximum black hole mass the code produces from roughly 60 to 100 solar masses. The LVK's fourth catalog lists binary black holes with component masses up to a median of 137 solar masses, above that modeled range. Gravitational-wave catalogs cannot settle the question alone, because stellar-mass binary black holes can be remnants of massive binary stars or can form through dynamical processes and mutual capture. LIGO said the spins of two events from the second part of the fourth run, GW241011 and GW241110, suggest second-generation black holes may be involved.

Population Codes Trade Stellar Detail for Speed, and Results Diverge

SEVN does not recompute a star's interior for every binary. It interpolates precomputed stellar tracks for properties such as total mass, radius and the masses of the helium and carbon-oxygen cores, then applies semi-analytic prescriptions for wind mass transfer, Roche-lobe overflow, common-envelope evolution, tides and gravitational-wave orbital decay. Maite Echeveste of the Osservatorio di Arcetri in Florence teaches the school's tutorial on SEVN.

POSYDON, built by a different collaboration, takes the opposite tradeoff. It uses the MESA stellar-structure code throughout each binary's life, and one MESA binary track can take more than 100 CPU hours, so POSYDON relies on pre-calculated grids that held nearly 120,000 detailed binary simulations in its first version. Pablo Marchant of Ghent University leads the school's tutorial on computational modeling of single and binary star evolution.

The consequence for readers is practical. A headline percentage for how merging black holes form is the output of one code and its assumptions about mass transfer, common envelopes, supernovae, tides and pair instability, the assumptions the SEVN team varied. Alejandra De Vito and Omar Benvenuto, both of Universidad de La Plata in Argentina, lecture at the school on massive-star evolution in binaries and on stellar structure and evolution.

Stellar Wind Models Turn Starlight Into Mass-Loss Measurements

Binary codes need inputs from observation, and hot massive stars lose mass through radiation-driven winds. Andreas Sander of the ZAH-ARI in Heidelberg both lectures on stellar atmosphere modeling and runs a tutorial on atmosphere and wind codes. In 2017, Sander and colleagues reported that their Potsdam Wolf-Rayet (PoWR) code had produced, for the first time, a hydrodynamically consistent model of a massive O star, solving the wind's motion together with the radiative transfer instead of prescribing it. Non-LTE treatment matters because Wolf-Rayet spectra form in strong winds, where emission lines arise from departures from local thermodynamic equilibrium.

Simón-Díaz and Berlanas teach the tutorial on quantitative spectroscopy of single massive stars. Simón-Díaz's IACOB project is a database of multi-epoch spectra of Galactic OB stars built at the IAC.

Spectra can mislead about companions, though. A 2024 IACOB study by Simón-Díaz and colleagues, based on more than 4,500 high-resolution spectra of 56 Galactic OB supergiants, found that intrinsic variability can produce peak-to-peak velocity swings of up to 20 to 25 km/s (about 12 to 16 miles per second) in late-O and early-B supergiants. The authors aimed to set empirical thresholds so that pulsating stars are not mistaken for single-line spectroscopic binaries, and they estimated that about 10% of OB supergiants are clearly single-line spectroscopic binaries.

Runaway Stars Test Supernova Kicks Against Cluster Ejections

Mar Carretero Castrillo, an ESO Fellow in Chile, will give the school's public talk on runaway stars on Tuesday, Nov. 24. ESO lists her among its 2025 fellows in Chile, with a December 2025 start. Runaway stars are massive stars flung from their birthplaces at high speed, and astronomers weigh two explanations: a push when a companion explodes as a supernova, or gravitational ejection during close encounters in dense young clusters.

In a Gaia-based study she led, summarized in the Sociedad Española de Astronomía bulletin in December 2024, Carretero Castrillo and colleagues identified 175 runaway stars, 106 of them O-type and 69 Be-type, about half newly identified as runaways. Runaways made up about 25.4% of the O-type stars and 5.2% of the Be-type stars in the catalogs, and some reached up to 200 km/s (124 miles per second). Because O-type runaways were more common and faster than Be-type ones, the results favor dynamical ejection from star clusters over the binary supernova scenario, the bulletin says. The study earned her third prize in the 2024 Vanguardia de la Ciencia contest, and she is from Lanzarote.

A January 2026 follow-up in Astronomy & Astrophysics, led by Carretero-Castrillo, combined Gaia measurements with IACOB spectra for 214 O-type stars. Most runaways rotate slowly, and the data are consistent with binary supernovae dominating among fast rotators, while the fastest-moving runaways tend to be single stars, which suggests ejection from young clusters. The team also examined twelve runaway single-lined binaries, three of which are known high-mass X-ray binaries.

Teide Visit Wednesday Precedes Optional La Palma Trip Saturday

Participants are scheduled to visit the Teide Observatory in Tenerife on Wednesday, Nov. 18, and an optional trip to the Roque de los Muchachos Observatory on La Palma is scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 21, according to the IAC event page. The Teide Observatory sits at 2,390 meters (about 7,840 feet) on Mount Teide and has been operated by the IAC since 1964. Berlanas described observatory visits as an established tradition of the IAC's Winter Schools.

Three Free Public Events Run Nov. 24 and Nov. 26 in La Laguna

All three events are free and open to the public until capacity is reached. Times below are Eastern Time, with local Tenerife time in parentheses.

  • Tuesday, Nov. 24, 12:30 p.m. ET (5:30 p.m. local): Carretero Castrillo's talk at the Museo de la Ciencia y el Cosmos, titled "Entre erupciones y golpes de mar: observando estrellas fugitivas desde el cielo de Canarias," roughly "Between eruptions and sea surges: observing runaway stars from the Canary skies."
  • Thursday, Nov. 26, 12:30 p.m. to 1:30 p.m. ET (5:30 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. local): A special edition of Del cielo a la tesis at the same museum, in which school participants present their massive-star research.
  • Thursday, Nov. 26, 2:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET (7:00 p.m. to 9:00 p.m. local): A special Astronomy on Tap edition at El Búho de La Laguna, with short talks by attendees.

Del cielo a la tesis is a monthly series organized by PhD students of the IAC and the University of La Laguna, with two short talks by early-career IAC researchers at the museum. Astronomy on Tap Canary Islands, known as AstroTragos, is run by IAC astronomers at El Búho on Calle Catedral and is listed as meeting on the first Thursday of the month, so the Nov. 26 session is a special edition.

The school's lecture slides and videos are to be posted on its website. When the final fourth-run catalog arrives in December, the useful questions for readers are which assumptions any claim about how black holes merge used for mass transfer, common envelopes, overshooting and pair instability, and whether another code reaches a different answer.

Frequently Asked Questions

What counts as a massive star?

Astronomers generally mean stars born with more than eight times the Sun's mass. Their ultraviolet radiation, winds and supernovae shape the interstellar medium and enrich it with heavy elements.

Do all massive stars end in a supernova?

Not necessarily. If a core is too massive, a black hole can form with no visible explosion, and some red supergiants have faded without one, such as N6946-BH1. The process that revives the stalled shock wave in core-collapse supernovae is also described as not clearly understood, and other theories besides neutrino heating have been proposed.

Can gravitational-wave catalogs alone show how black hole mergers form?

Not on their own. Stellar-mass binary black holes may be remnants of massive binary stars or may form through dynamical processes and capture, so models of stellar and binary evolution are needed to connect detections to origins. The SEVN results above show those models can disagree, even with identical binary-evolution parameters.

Can people outside Tenerife follow the lectures?

The IAC says lecture slides and videos will be posted on the school website, and participants can present their own work as online posters and pitch talks. The three public events take place at venues in La Laguna.
